Seminar Title:

Multiple Stages of Magma Generation and Complex Tectonic Evolution of the Neotethyan Oceanic Lithosphere: Insights from Crustal Rocks of Nidar Ophiolite, Ladakh, NW Himalaya

Seminar Type:

Departmental Seminar

Department:

Speaker Type:

Contact:

Abstract:

Nidar ophiolite complex (NOC) of Ladakh, NW Himalaya preserves a diverse suite of crustal rocks including basalt, gabbro, dolerite and plagiogranites, providing an opportunity to study the magmatic and tectonic evolution of the Neotethyan oceanic crust. In this study, we integrate mineral chemistry, whole-rock major and trace-element geochemistry to constrain the petrogenesis and tectonic evolution of the crustal rocks in Nidar ophiolite complex. Gabbros of NOC exhibit MORB to IAT chemical affinities and record crystallization temperature of 1092- 1121°C and pressure of ~6.5–7.3 kbar, indicating deep crustal to upper mantle depth magmatic processes. Similarly, basalts yield comparable temperatures of 1106–1119°C at pressure 6.9–7.3 kbar, suggesting a close relationship between the early basaltic melts and their plutonic equivalents. In contrast, dolerites show predominantly N- MORB affinity and crystallized at comparatively lower pressures (~3.7–6.2 kbar) and temperatures (~986–1079°C), suggesting emplacement during a late stage of oceanic crustal evolution. The plagiogranite exhibits variable N-MORB to OIB-like trace-element characteristics, indicating an origin through complex magmatic processes rather than simple differentiation of a single parental magma. Basalt, gabbro, and dolerite exhibit primary igneous assemblages dominated by clinopyroxene and feldspar. The gabbros contain labradorite with subordinate orthoclase, with clinopyroxene Mg# value of 0.79–0.92, indicating relatively primitive to moderately evolved mafic magmas. In contrast, basalts and dolerites are dominated by albite, with clinopyroxene Mg# values of 0.73–0.92 and 0.34–0.63, respectively. The substantially lower Mg# of clinopyroxene in the dolerites indicates a more evolved character compared to basalt and gabbro, consistent with their relatively lower crystallization temperatures and pressures. The integrated geochemical and P–T constraints therefore reveal a complex, polyphase magmatic history of NOC crustal rocks involving a SSZ to back-arc spreading followed by renewed MORB-like magmatism and subsequent crustal enrichment, reflecting a dynamic evolution of the Neotethyan oceanic lithosphere.
